items_missed: No agenda at the top of the call. The roadmap arrived roughly halfway through — 'Alright I'll walk you through the basic pricing first Patricia... and then I'll send you an estimate later. Sounds good.' — and it carried no timeframe. The first eight minutes were an unstructured inventory hunt with no stated plan, so the customer never knew whether she was on a 3-minute or a 15-minute call.

Move-date availability never actually checked. Amy referenced 'your requested date, Saturday, September 19th' and pitched cheaper Sunday/Mon–Thu rates, but never confirmed Einstein has crews open that Saturday — and this is a 4-mover, 2-truck job on a peak-rate weekend day.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This was the single biggest content miss: the entire call was the customer worrying about high-value, awkward items — a 250 lb sauna, a squat rack, a rolling workbench, two refrigerators — and the word 'insurance' appeared only once, buried in the included-items list.

No 'pricing is super simple' framing and no full no-hidden-fees pitch. Amy covered 'no credit card fees, no, no disassemble fees' and the free service zone, but never said 'no hidden fees,' never named the fuel surcharge or transportation fee, and never used the simple-pricing opener.

Clock start never explained. She gave the 2.5-hour minimum and the 15-minute proration but never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens — a gap that matters on a two-truck job where the crews arrive together.

Save Your Ass speech never given, and the customer handed her the perfect opening. Patricia said 'The plan is we finished packing before anyone come before you come?' and Amy answered only 'I'll just wait for the picture then I'll work out an estimate for you.' No prep-equals-lower-bill framing, no consolidation examples (loose drawer items, garden tools, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip. The only prep ask was feasibility-driven — 'would you be able to disassemble it in advance or do you need our movers to do that?' — never tied to money.

No booking attempt at all. The customer had a firm date, said the rate 'seems reasonable' and confirmed the math herself — 'okay, that makes sense for six hours' — and the call ended with 'I'll email you the estimate' and no ask. Never said 'we have availability, want me to lock that in?'
No deposit required was never mentioned. On a $2,664–$3,108 job that is the one line that makes saying yes free, and it was the natural answer to a customer who needed to check with her husband.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections.' Given that the estimate rests on a hand-counted inventory of 40–60 boxes plus late-added refrigerators, washer and dryer, the verify-in-writing step was needed here more than on a normal call.

No closing 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the two questions checks ('Do you have any questions so far?', 'does that make sense? So far do you have any questions?') both landed mid-pricing, and the call closed straight into 'Okay, thank you so much... you have a great evening.'

Hours and contact info never given. Patricia had to work out how to reach Amy on her own mid-call — 'how do I text you when I'm on the phone with you? You're not a contact' — then read the number back herself from the email. Amy confirmed neither her direct line nor office hours, on a call that ends in a pending callback.

Probe gaps: stairs or floors at either address, walk distance from truck to door, parking or access at either home, additional stops, storage stops, and long-walk/narrow-hallway considerations were never asked. Patricia volunteered the only stairs signal herself — 'it doesn't need to go upstairs or anything like that' about the workbench.

Moving stressors never asked. Amy read the quote form's concerns field aloud ('Moving concerns in waste doble and plates') but never asked Patricia what she was worried about — on a move where the customer had already volunteered anxiety about the sauna twice.

Customer's direct question got no answer. Patricia asked 'What if we don't want to take it apart, is there an option?' and the transcript shows only 'Then got question.' / 'It is.' / 'Yeah.' — she moved on to pricing and only circled back later with the manager's no.
Insurance never explained as a product. No No Worries $2,000 figure, no 60¢/lb baseline — just 'includes taxes, insurance, and the gas.'

Clarity and pace. Amy's side of the transcript garbles far more than the customer's — 'basic bay success', 'we will bring movie brackets shrink wrap Bens. Doggies', 'we would need towards no for us to handle the disassemble', 'it might video breaker for you'. Some is ASR, but the density on one side only points to speed and diction.

1850 sqft plus a garage gym, squat rack, sauna, patio furniture and 40–60 boxes is the virtual-walkthrough profile, and the customer said so herself — 'while it's under 2000 square feet... it's probably like a 2000 square foot home.' It was quoted over the phone instead of routed.
top_strength: The inventory and estimate work was genuinely strong, and it was the part of the call Amy chose to own. She defused the customer's opening anxiety instantly and correctly — Patricia led with 'I left off a refrig. Two refrigerators and a washer and dryer on my list... that can make a difference for the quote' and Amy came back with 'the good thing is for hourly base so if you have less, if you have more items that's totally fine.' She then probed the hard items properly rather than guessing: asked for a photo of the sauna ('I wanna double-check with our team first if that's something we can commit to'), chased the actual weight until the customer found it ('it does 250 pounds item weight'), gave the real boundary on the workbench ('so it's not more than 500 comms we can definitely move it'), and held the safety line on propane — 'we don't handle anything that has gas you know for safety reasons.' She escalated live to a branch manager mid-call and came back with a real answer instead of a maybe. The estimate itself is the best-built section: she gave the baseline for the home size ('for the house the size we would just need one truck three movers for about six to eight hours'), then walked the customer through why this job is bigger, using the drive as her reasoning — 'the new home is only seven miles away... but I just wanna make sure that we don't have to go back and forth. So I would suggest sending four movers two trucks' — named her own bias out loud ('If I'm being a bit conservative'), gave both ends of the range in dollars, and framed it honestly: 'this is just an estimate... you are not the bound by the numbers at the end of the day you only pay for the actual time.' She also volunteered cheaper days unprompted ($105 Sunday, $104 Mon–Thu against $111 Saturday), which is real budget-conscious selling, not a script line.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Amy did the whole job and then didn't ask for it. She had a firm date, a firm price, and a customer who confirmed the math out loud — 'so it's $111 times essentially four movers... times six hours so $2,600 and okay, $64. Okay, okay, that makes sense for six hours' — which is a buying signal, not an acknowledgment. The line she needed right there was: 'Perfect, Patricia. There's no deposit and nothing due today, so I can hold Saturday the 19th for you right now and you can still cancel or change it free — want me to lock it in while we sort out the sauna?' Instead the call ended on 'I'll email you the estimate,' with the customer needing to talk to her husband and Einstein holding nothing. Note that 'no deposit' is the exact answer to 'I have to talk to my husband about it' — it removes the reason to wait — and it was never said on this call. Second priority: three of the five differentiators went unspoken on a call that was begging for all three. A customer moving a 250 lb sauna, a squat rack and two refrigerators needed 'That's exactly what our No Worries Damage Coverage is for — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage'; a customer who is a first-time Einstein buyer needed Meet Your Mover; and a Saturday two-truck job needed the On-Time Guarantee. Third: the Save Your Ass speech was left on the table after the customer volunteered that she'd be fully packed. That was the moment for 'That's the single best thing you can do for your bill, Patricia — every hour we don't spend packing is an hour off the total. Two more things that shave real time: empty the loose stuff out of drawers into your rubbermaids and get the photos off the walls, and anything small and fragile that fits in your car, take a carload over yourself. Does that make sense?' Business risks to close today: (1) The final commitment is genuinely unclear — 'this estimate includes moving the sign-up. But should be disassembled in advance and we won't handle the a' — Patricia has been told the sauna is in the quote, must be pre-disassembled by her, and cannot be disassembled by us, and she is now deciding with her husband whether that's a deal breaker. That needs one unambiguous written sentence in the email, or this job is lost or disputed. (2) Patricia asked 'What if we don't want to take it apart, is there an option?' and never got an answer — the honest answer, including whether we can refer a sauna installer, is what wins this move. (3) Amanda's policy check: an 1850 sqft home with a garage gym, sauna and patio furniture was quoted over the phone rather than routed to a virtual walkthrough, and Amy priced two trucks and four movers off a text photo and a customer's own square footage. This is the exact profile the walkthrough gate exists for, and it is also an estimate-accuracy exposure on a $2,664–$3,108 job.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and unhurried — 'Of course, of course', 'No problem', 'Yes, ma'am', and a genuine unprompted compliment ('I love it. You're very comprehensive with the list. Thank you.') kept a stressed customer relaxed through a five-minute wait and a no answer, and Patricia stayed positive to the end ('Okay, you too. Yeah, you too. Bye now.'); the one dent is the unanswered 'is there an option?' moment, which reads as talked past.
audio_review_reason: Amy's side of the transcript garbles heavily while the customer's stays clean ('basic bay success', 'movie brackets shrink wrap Bens. Doggies', 'we would need towards no for us to handle the disassemble'), so the clarity-and-pace bonus point and the what's-included recital cannot be fairly judged from text; audio is also needed to confirm whether she actually answered Patricia's 'What if we don't want to take it apart' question or spoke over it.
